INFANT 1 · LESSON 3

Colors & First Objects for Babies 3–4 Months

Age 3–4 MonthsSubject SeeClass Infant 1Duration 2–5 minutes

Around three to four months, many babies begin to notice colour and reach toward the world. This class pairs bold red, yellow and blue with a few familiar objects — a ball, a cup, a spoon, an apple, a teddy — shown one at a time in short, parent-led sessions.

Name what you see if you like, and let your baby look for as long as they want. There is no need to test anything or expect a response: this is shared looking, not a quiz.

PARENT INSTRUCTIONS

How to use this activity

Choose a time when your baby is awake, calm and comfortable. Show one card at a time and give your baby time to look. You can name familiar objects naturally as you show them, but there is no need to test your baby or expect a response.

This lesson introduces bold red, yellow and blue alongside simple familiar objects. Keep sessions short and follow your baby’s interest.

Stop when your baby looks away, becomes tired, fussy or loses interest.

Every baby develops differently. Kiddo School age ranges are guides, not tests or developmental deadlines.

TRY TOGETHER

Little things to say.

Prompts for you, not for the cards — say them softly while your baby looks.

  • Look at the red circle.
  • Here is the ball.
  • Can you see the cup?
  • This is an apple.
  • Where is the sun?
  • Hello, teddy.

    Red circle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson starts the colour chapter of card time: one day, one colour, one real red thing found in your home. Everything else — matching, naming, sorting — is years away, and that is exactly on schedule.

    What is this?

    Red is a colour, and the card gives it in its simplest costume: one large, bold circle. At 3–4 months your baby’s colour vision is still warming up, and red is the shade that lands earliest — the natural first colour to offer.

    What does it mean?

    The eye’s colour sensors come online in stages, and the long red wavelengths register before the rest of the spectrum. That physiology is why so many baby sets lead with red: you are showing the colour your baby is best equipped to see.

    What does the child need to know?

    The plan is deliberately small: this red card today, its yellow twin tomorrow, its blue cousin the day after. One colour at a time gives each shade room to be noticed. And every session gets a real-world twin — one red thing from your home, held up for two seconds.

    Why this matters

    Colour is a property, not an object, and property-thinking starts here: the baby meets "red" as something a circle can be, a jumper can be, a book can be. That idea — one word stretching across many things — is the seed of all later categories.

    What it teaches

    Colour discrimination, visual attention on a single bold target, real-world transfer (card to object), and narration listening — your baby hearing one colour word attached to many different things.

    Words to learn

    redcirclelookcolourroundfound it

    Say this to your child

    “"Red! Here is a big round circle in red. And look — here is my red sock. Red on the card, red in my hand. Red is out in the world today, and you are finding it."”

    Step by step

    1. Choose an alert window after a feed, settle your baby and show the red circle at close focusing range, filling a good slice of the view.
    2. Say its name twice, slowly and warmly: "Red. A big red circle." Then hold still and let the looking happen.
    3. Swatting or batting at the card? Wonderful — bring it a fingertip closer so the swipe can land, with your hand behind it the whole time.
    4. Now the twin: grab one red thing within arm’s reach — a sock, a book, a toy — and hold it beside the card. The word is the same; the sizes are not.
    5. Close the session there. One colour, one object, two minutes; tomorrow belongs to yellow.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is exactly one large red circle and nothing else — say that much. The live noticing is richer: does your baby’s gaze jump between card and real red object? That little trip is transfer, happening in real time.

    Ask your child

    Watch the pairing: when the real red thing arrives, do the eyes cross to it, or stay loyal to the card? Does a swat come when the object is near? Wonder aloud: "I wonder which red you prefer — the flat one or the fuzzy one."

    What your child can say or do

    Long stares that flick between card and sock, an arm swing that grazes the card, a fresh kick of interest when the real object lands, or a calm blink and nothing more — all four are normal replies at 3–4 months.

    Out in the real world

    Red waits all over the house: a mug on the counter, the spine of a book, the tomato in the fruit bowl. Each time you pass one during the day, tap it and say "red" once. The card taught the word; the house repeats it for free.

    Try it together

    One-colour day: pick red as today’s tiny theme and narrate every red thing you meet out loud — red sock at dressing, red cup at lunch, red leaf at the window. Your baby does nothing but listen and look, which is everything.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did one real red object actually join the session, and did you manage to keep the whole thing under five minutes? Small and repeatable is the design; long and dutiful is how card time dies.

    Parent tips

    Resist adding more colours to speed things up — parallel colours cancel each other out at this age. If your baby seems bored, move the card a little, not the plan. Repetition feels dull to you and builds exactly nothing but memory for them.

    Staying safe

    The adult holds the card for every second of every session — at this age everything that lands in a hand heads for the mouth, and cards are not teethers. Real red props get chosen for size too: bigger than a fist, nothing that can snap or shed.

    This lesson pairs with the Red circle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & First Objects (Infant 1).

    Yellow circle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Yesterday was red; today the circle comes back in yellow. This lesson uses that single change to smuggle in the biggest idea of the set: what the word "colour" is actually about.

    What is this?

    Yellow is the second colour card: the same round shape your baby met in red, now in a bright, sunny shade. The shape staying constant is the whole trick — the only thing that changed is the colour, so colour is what gets noticed.

    What does it mean?

    Babies spot change before they spot categories. When everything about an image stays put except one feature, the growing brain flags that feature as "what this thing is about". Two circles, one red and one yellow, quietly define colour for your baby.

    What does the child need to know?

    Show yellow on its own first, then bring the red card alongside. Name them in turn — red... yellow — with a pause between, so each word lands on its own colour. Do not expect your baby to match or prefer anything; preference is a bonus, not a goal.

    Why this matters

    A baby who has seen "same shape, different colour" twice has the beginnings of comparison: how are these alike, how are they not? That question will one day sort animals, letters, numbers and people. It starts with two paper circles.

    What it teaches

    Colour discrimination, same-and-different noticing at the earliest level, visual comparison across two cards, and turn-taking in narration.

    Words to learn

    yellowredcirclesamedifferentsunny

    Say this to your child

    “"Yellow! A big yellow circle, bright as the morning. And here comes our old friend — red. Red circle, yellow circle. The same shape in two different dresses. Look at them both, side by side."”

    Step by step

    1. Settle your baby and show the yellow circle alone at close range, naming it twice: "Yellow. A big yellow circle."
    2. Give it a good long look — at least ten seconds of nothing but the card and your quiet.
    3. Bring the red circle into view beside it, matched for height and distance, and name them in turns: "Red... and yellow."
    4. Let your baby’s eyes travel between them as long as they like; a slow sway of one card restarts a stalled gaze.
    5. Finish with whichever colour held the longer look — say that colour’s name once more as the last word, then tidy away.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is one large yellow circle, the red card’s exact twin in a new shade — say that much. Then watch the real event: do the eyes move between the two colours, or settle on one? Whichever happens is your baby’s honest answer today.

    Ask your child

    Watch the travel: does the gaze cross from yellow to red and back, or camp on one? Does the same colour win two days running? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if you like the new one best because it is new."

    What your child can say or do

    Side-to-side looking between the cards, a longer gaze on one colour, an excited leg-kick when the second card appears, or a drowsy drift that ends things early — every version counts, and the drift is a full stop, not a fail.

    Out in the real world

    Yellow lives in kitchens and walks: a banana on the counter, a rubber duck on the bath edge, dandelions in the grass. One tap, one "yellow" each time — the second meeting of the word does more than the first ever could.

    Try it together

    Lap swap: show yellow, then red, then yellow again across your lap, letting your body be the card stand. Your baby’s head turns become the game — you are strengthening neck control and colour memory in the same five minutes.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the two colours actually meet this session, and did you pause between their names? The pause is what keeps the words from blurring into one — say them like two separate gifts.

    Parent tips

    Keep the shape talk minimal — the circles are alike on purpose, and that is enough. If your baby ignores yellow entirely, do not chase it; tomorrow’s blue is a fresh chance. Never audition colours against each other like a contest.

    Staying safe

    Two cards in play means two cards in your hands or folded away — nothing rests on the baby’s chest or beside them on the mat. Swats happen: accept them against the held card, and check for dented edges before the next session.

    This lesson pairs with the Yellow circle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & First Objects (Infant 1).

    Blue circle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Today the family grows to three. This lesson adds blue, then walks your baby’s eyes along the whole trio — a naming parade that becomes the backbone of colour weeks to come.

    What is this?

    Blue is the third colour card: one bold blue circle, twin to the red and yellow ones. With it, the set holds the classic trio that baby toys, blocks and books have used for generations.

    What does it mean?

    Three colours make a system. One colour is a fact, two are a comparison, but three start to feel like a set — and your baby, without any words at all, is absorbing that colours come in families and that each has its own name.

    What does the child need to know?

    The parade is the game: line the three cards up in a row at close range and name each one as your finger taps it, one colour per slow breath. Your baby’s eyes will hop, drift or fixate — all of it is the lesson. Naming colours comes years from now; hearing them named is now.

    Why this matters

    Ordered naming — left to right, one at a time — is the same skill that later turns into counting, reading and following instructions. The traffic-light line-up is your baby’s first experience of information arriving in an order.

    What it teaches

    Colour recognition through repetition, left-to-right visual scanning, listening to sequenced naming, and sustained attention across a multi-card display.

    Words to learn

    bluethreecolourslinefirstlast

    Say this to your child

    “"Blue! Now we have three. Red, yellow, blue — a little rainbow on my lap. I will touch each one: red here, yellow here, blue here. Three colours, three friends, all looking at you."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the blue circle alone first, at close focusing range, and name it: "Blue. A big blue circle."
    2. Let the new colour earn its own full look before any reunion — ten unhurried seconds.
    3. Now line up red, yellow and blue in a row across your lap or the mat, evenly spaced and firmly in view.
    4. Tap and name in order — "red... yellow... blue" — one colour per slow breath, then run the parade again if the eyes are still working.
    5. End the session with the middle card or the whole row as the final image, then pack the trio away together.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is one large blue circle, matching its red and yellow siblings — say that much. The richer show is behavioural: when the parade runs, do your baby’s eyes follow your tapping finger from card to card? That following is the skill being built.

    Ask your child

    Watch the parade: does the gaze shadow your finger along the row, or jump ahead on its own? Does one colour always get the longest stop? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if the order matters to you, or just the colours."

    What your child can say or do

    Eyes hopping card to card with your taps, a favourite colour that collects every long look, full-body wriggles when the row appears, or a yawn that ends the parade early — every one is a normal day at this age.

    Out in the real world

    Blue gets discovered in showers and cupboards: the sky through the window, the bath towel, a favourite mug. Say "blue" each time you pass one today. Three cards, then a whole house of the same word — that is how vocabulary grows.

    Try it together

    Colour traffic game: hold the three cards in a fan and bring one to the front at a time, naming it as it arrives — red day, yellow day, blue day. Unpredictable order keeps the eyes alert; the naming stays the same.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did each colour get its name at least three times today, in order, at baby pace? If your own pace sped up, shorten the row rather than rushing the words — two colours named well beats three named fast.

    Parent tips

    If three cards at once overloads your baby — darting eyes, fussing — drop back to two and rebuild the trio over the week. Vary which colour sits first in the line so position does not become the memory.

    Staying safe

    A row of cards lies flat on your lap or the mat under your hand, never propped upright where it could topple towards the baby. Session length stays short; three colours is a full working set for a 3–4-month brain.

    This lesson pairs with the Blue circle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & First Objects (Infant 1).

    Three colors — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    One card holds all three colours at once. This lesson treats it the way it deserves: not a first card but a finale — the review that ties a colour week together.

    What is this?

    The three colours card puts red, yellow and blue together on a single bold page. After your baby has met each shade on its own, this card is the reunion — everything the week taught, in one view.

    What does it mean?

    Review works differently for babies than for children: there is nothing to recall, only to re-meet. Seeing the three colours together after days of single colours lets the brain notice both the togetherness and the differences, without any effort from anyone.

    What does the child need to know?

    The pointing rhythm is the heart of this lesson: one colour per slow breath, three breaths for the whole card. Slowness is not laziness here — it is what lets a 3–4-month gaze find each shade before the next one is named.

    Why this matters

    Ending a run of sessions on a summary image teaches the shape of learning itself: things get met one at a time, then seen together. That rhythm — parts, then whole — is how your child will one day meet letters, then words.

    What it teaches

    Visual consolidation of the colour trio, slow sequential pointing, breath-paced shared attention, and the comfort of a familiar finale card.

    Words to learn

    redyellowbluetogetherbreatheall done

    Say this to your child

    “"Red, yellow, blue — all three friends on one page. I will say hello to each one, slowly, slowly. Red... yellow... blue. There they are, all together. What a colourful card to finish with."”

    Step by step

    1. Bring the card out at the end of a session, not the start, and announce it like a treat: "All three colours! Together."
    2. Hold it steady at close range and simply let your baby take the whole busy page in for a few seconds.
    3. Point at the red with one fingertip and say "red" as you breathe out; rest a full breath before the next colour.
    4. Point yellow the same way, then blue — three shades, three breaths, no rushing anywhere.
    5. Lower the card, say your closing word — "all done" — and let that be the end; this card should always finish things, never open them.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork shows the three bold colours sharing one page — say that much. What deserves noticing is your baby’s stamina: three named colours is a longer attention job than one. Did today’s run last longer than last week’s? That is your progress line.

    Ask your child

    Watch the pace: does your baby’s gaze keep up with a breath-slow pointing rhythm, or fall behind at the third colour? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if we should give blue its own extra breath next time."

    What your child can say or do

    Eyes trailing your finger from shade to shade, a settled body that matches your slow pace, a startle-blink when the busy card first arrives, or looking away before the trio finishes — all normal; the card will wait.

    Out in the real world

    Things that come in threes fill the house: the traffic lights on your walk, three mugs on the shelf, the trio of bath toys on the tub edge. Pointing out real threes keeps this card’s idea in circulation all week.

    Try it together

    Breath trio at bath time: name three coloured things in the water or on the tiles — one per breath, exactly like the card. The rhythm transfers, and bath becomes a gentle rehearsal room without a single card in sight.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did you keep to one colour per breath, and did this card genuinely close the session rather than open it? Both are discipline points — the design only works if the finale stays a finale.

    Parent tips

    If your baby handles the trio easily, resist adding a fourth colour or a faster pace; the value is in the calm repetition, not the difficulty. Save this card for weeks when all three single colours have had their days.

    Staying safe

    A busier card holds attention longer, which can mean a drowsier baby by the end — finish before the yawns turn to fussing, and move the card well clear as sleep approaches. Pointing fingers stay gentle: taps on the card, never on the baby.

    This lesson pairs with the Three colors flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & First Objects (Infant 1).

    Ball — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This is the card most likely to connect instantly: the thing on the page is the thing already in your baby’s toy basket. This lesson makes the link out loud.

    What is this?

    A ball is a round toy that rolls and bounces, and at 3–4 months your baby has almost certainly watched one, batted one or gummed one. The card gives that familiar friend a clear, still portrait.

    What does it mean?

    Familiar objects make strong cards because half the learning is already done: your baby knows what a ball feels like to chase with their eyes. The card adds the name and the look; the toy box supplies the rest.

    What does the child need to know?

    The magic move is rolling a real ball gently across your baby’s field of view right after the card — the picture names it, the rolling proves it. And when a swat lands on the card, treat it as a milestone: batting at what interests you is brand-new engineering.

    Why this matters

    Object play is the beginning of physics: things move, things stop, things come back. Naming the ball while it moves teaches your baby that words can describe action, not just still pictures — an idea language will need forever.

    What it teaches

    Object recognition, visual tracking of a rolling target, early reach-and-bat coordination, and word-action pairing — the card says it, the world shows it.

    Words to learn

    ballrollroundbouncycatchagain

    Say this to your child

    “"Ball! Here is the picture ball, round and bright. And here comes a real one — rolling, rolling, rolling... and it stopped. Let us roll it again. Ball is such a good word."”

    Step by step

    1. Settle your baby and show the card at close range with its name: "Ball. Round and ready to roll."
    2. Give the picture a good look — then fetch a real ball that is big, light and clean enough for baby eyes and hands.
    3. Roll it slowly across the floor or mat within your baby’s view, saying "ball" as it moves, once, not on repeat.
    4. Let the ball stop, then bring it back into view; if a hand swings towards it, let the touch happen.
    5. Finish with the card again — picture, world, picture — so the loop closes and the word has been heard twice in two forms.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork shows a bright, friendly ball — say that much. The live noticing is better: did the eyes follow the real ball on its roll, and did the gaze return to the card afterwards? Picture-world-picture is the circuit you are watching for.

    Ask your child

    Watch the roll: do the eyes track the ball all the way, or lose it when it slows? Does the swat aim for the card, the real ball, or both? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if the moving ball or the still card holds you longer today."

    What your child can say or do

    Intent tracking of the rolling ball, a triumphant bat that connects with the card, both hands meeting on the real ball, or a startled blink at the first roll — all normal at 3–4 months, and the bat is a small masterpiece.

    Out in the real world

    Balls fill the weeks ahead: the one in the pram basket, the big one at baby group, the dog’s ball in the park. Each sighting is a one-word replay — "ball" — and the card has already done the teaching.

    Try it together

    Lap roll: sit your baby supported against you and roll a soft ball gently up their legs and back down, naming it each time. Body contact plus the word plus the movement makes this the richest ball lesson in the house.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did a real ball actually roll during the session, and did you let any swat or touch land without taking over? Both matter — the prop proves the word, and the touch belongs to the baby.

    Parent tips

    One roll per session is enough; three rolls is a circus. If your baby fixates on the real ball and drops the card, let it be — the card will win back attention tomorrow. Choose balls bigger than their fist, always.

    Staying safe

    Real balls for this age are big, light and clean — nothing small enough to swallow, nothing with a hard seam, nothing that was living in the dog’s bed. Card stays adult-held; rolled balls stay on the mat, away from faces.

    This lesson pairs with the Ball flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & First Objects (Infant 1).

    Cup — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Of everything in the set, the cup may be the object your baby knows best — it appears at every single feed. This lesson attaches its name to something already deeply familiar.

    What is this?

    A cup is a drinking vessel, and your baby has watched one work since birth: lifted, tipped, returning full. The card gives that daily companion a simple portrait, and the lesson gives it a name said out loud.

    What does it mean?

    Everyday-object cards look plain next to colourful toys, but plainness is their engine: familiarity means your baby already has feelings, memories and expectations around this object. The card is not introducing a thing — it is naming a relationship.

    What does the child need to know?

    The replay is the lesson: at the next feed or meal, hold up the real cup, say "cup" once with a smile, and let ten quiet seconds do the work. Repeating that tiny ritual daily beats any long session — the word rides on routine.

    Why this matters

    Words that arrive attached to comfort — food, drink, the people who provide them — get deep processing for free. Cup is one of the highest-value first words in any language precisely because it turns up when your baby is already content and attentive.

    What it teaches

    Object recognition, word-object mapping through daily repetition, anticipation (the cup means feeding is coming), and early routine awareness.

    Words to learn

    cupdrinkmilkcupfulhello cupall gone

    Say this to your child

    “"Cup! This is the picture of a cup, and look — here is our real cup, coming for milk. Card cup, real cup, same word. You drink from your cup every day. Hello, cup. Here you come again."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at close range in a calm moment and name it warmly: "Cup. You know cups — you see one every day."
    2. Trace the cup’s shape with your finger — round body, handle or not — and let your baby study it in silence.
    3. Bring the card back at the very next feed, before the real cup appears, and say "cup" once.
    4. Then lift the actual cup into view: "Here is our cup." Picture, then reality, ten seconds total.
    5. Repeat the pre-feed version daily for a week; by day three or four you may catch the flicker of recognition that makes this card famous.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a simple everyday cup — say that much, no decoration needed. The noticing worth keeping is behavioural: does your baby’s attention sharpen when the real cup appears after the card? Recognition at 3–4 months looks like brightening, not pointing.

    Ask your child

    Watch the pre-feed moment: does the gaze move to the card when you say the word, or hold on you? Does the real cup collect a longer look than the card? Wonder aloud: "I wonder which one feels like the real cup to you."

    What your child can say or do

    Brightening eyes at the word, a head turn towards the arriving real cup, hungry rooting that mistakes the lesson for lunch, or both hands waving as the feed begins — all of it is your baby telling you the routine is meaningful.

    Out in the real world

    Cups surround the day: the one you drink from, the little one waiting in the cupboard for weaning months, cups at cafes and grandma’s table. Every sighting is a replay of this card, for months to come.

    Try it together

    Cup hello: at each feed, lift the cup into your baby’s view before it starts its work and greet it — "hello, cup" — in the same voice every time. Within a week the greeting itself will make your baby look. That is ritual, memory and language in one.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the word "cup" get said at a real feed today, not just at card time? The card is the rehearsal; the feed is the performance. One performance a day is the whole curriculum.

    Parent tips

    Do not rush the card into weaning stories or sippy-cup shopping — this lesson is about the name, not the milestone. If feeds are chaotic, run the card hello at the calmest feed of the day and skip the rest guilt-free.

    Staying safe

    Hot drinks and babies do not share a lap — the cup you name is the baby’s feed cup or a cool empty one, never your boiling tea. Cards stay out of the feed zone entirely: milk and paper do not mix.

    This lesson pairs with the Cup flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & First Objects (Infant 1).

    Spoon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The spoon card belongs to the future as much as the present: one day soon this object will run your mealtimes. This lesson gives the word a head start.

    What is this?

    A spoon is the small scoop that brings food to mouths, and your baby has watched you use one at every meal of their life. The card shows it plainly; the lesson says its name out loud, at card time and at table time.

    What does it mean?

    Spoon sits in a special family of words — the tool words — that children learn through watching them work. Naming the tool before the baby wields it builds a bridge: when self-feeding starts, the word is already old news and the object already has a story.

    What does the child need to know?

    Two settings, one word: the card at quiet time, then the real spoon held up at the next meal — "spoon" — with a smile. The flicker of recognition you may catch is real progress at this age. Keep both meetings under a minute each.

    Why this matters

    Mealtimes give this word more performances than any other card could buy: several shows a day, every day, with food as the co-star. Repetition in different places is what teaches a baby that words belong to objects everywhere, not just on paper.

    What it teaches

    Tool recognition, word-object mapping across settings (card and table), mealtime attention, and the earliest narrative habit — you, supplying words for what happens next.

    Words to learn

    spoonscooptastyhere comesmoreyum

    Say this to your child

    “"Spoon! Here is the picture spoon, long and shiny. And at lunchtime — look — here is our real spoon. Same word, same scoop. The spoon brings the food, all the way to your mouth. Here comes the spoon."”

    Step by step

    1. At a calm moment, show the card at close range: "Spoon. The little scoop that brings the food."
    2. Trace its shape aloud — the bowl at the end, the long handle — while your baby looks.
    3. At the next meal, lift the real spoon into view before it starts working and say "spoon" once, warmly.
    4. Let the spoon do its ordinary job without commentary; the word has already been planted.
    5. Repeat the pre-meal greeting daily — the card can visit the table edge (out of grab range) or stay on the shelf; the real spoon carries the lesson.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a bold, simple spoon — say that much. The live noticing: when you hold up the real spoon at mealtime, do your baby’s eyes lock on, and does their body lean towards the incoming food? That leaning is anticipation — learning wearing its work clothes.

    Ask your child

    Watch the two settings: does the word "spoon" collect attention in both places, or only at the table? Wonder aloud: "I wonder when you will start opening your mouth at the word alone — I am watching for it."

    What your child can say or do

    Locking eyes on the raised spoon, a full-body wriggle as food approaches, mouth-opening practise at the sight of it, or a hand batting towards the shiny bowl — all of it is mealtime literacy being born, months before the first self-fed bite.

    Out in the real world

    Spoons appear all day: yours at breakfast, the little weaning spoon waiting in the drawer, the big wooden one that stirs the pot. Each glimpse can carry a one-word replay — "spoon" — making your kitchen the card’s second home.

    Try it together

    Spoon parade: at each meal, bring the spoon into view from the same side with the same greeting — "here comes the spoon" — and let the arrival be mildly theatrical. Predictable shows build anticipation, and anticipation is attention in disguise.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the word "spoon" land at a real meal today as well as at card time? Two settings, one word — that is the entire method. If card time was skipped but the meal greeting happened, the day still counts.

    Parent tips

    Keep the card away from the actual eating — a card on the tray becomes a chew toy and the lesson becomes laundry. The table-edge placement only works within your reach, never the baby’s.

    Staying safe

    Real spoons for babies are the soft-tipped weaning kind, and they stay with the grown-up until feeding time — a spoon waved by a 3–4-month-old ends up in an eye or a throat. Card and food never share a surface.

    This lesson pairs with the Spoon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & First Objects (Infant 1).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & FIRST OBJECTS · AGES 3–4 MONTHS

    Apple — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The apple card does triple duty: it is a colour lesson, a shape lesson and a preview of the fruit bowl. This lesson uses its best trick — the same object, two sizes.

    What is this?

    An apple is a round fruit, red or green, that lives in your kitchen and will one day live in your baby’s hand. The card shows one shiny example; the lesson brings the real thing alongside for the comparison.

    What does it mean?

    Picture-to-world transfer is a genuine cognitive leap: understanding that a flat image stands for a real thing. Babies build it through exactly this exercise — same object, same word, two presentations — repeated casually over months.

    What does the child need to know?

    Hold the real apple right beside the card at close range and let your baby look between them. Say "apple" for each. Do not rush tasting — your baby is months from solids — and do not expect the comparison to look like anything. The wiring happens quietly.

    Why this matters

    Every picture book your child will ever love depends on this skill: flat apple means apple. Building it now, with an object this familiar, means the skill will be waiting when books arrive — and it costs ten seconds a day.

    What it teaches

    Picture-world transfer, size comparison (big card, small fruit), colour and shape reinforcement, and vocabulary attached to a multi-sense object your baby will soon hold, smell and taste.

    Words to learn

    appleroundredshinyfruitsame

    Say this to your child

    “"Apple! Here is the picture apple, and here is a real apple from our kitchen. Big apple, small apple — the same round shape. Red and shiny on the card, red and shiny in my hand. Apples are everywhere."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at close range and name it: "Apple. A round, shiny apple."
    2. Let the picture get its full look — then fetch a real apple from the kitchen, clean and dry.
    3. Hold the apple beside the card, matched height if you can, and say "apple" as the eyes move between them.
    4. Turn the real apple slowly in your hand — a different angle, the same apple — then bring the card back for the final look.
    5. Put the fruit away and end with the card; the picture should get the last word today.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a bright, round apple — say that much. The live noticing is the transfer itself: does your baby’s gaze travel between card and fruit, or settle on one? Even a single crossing is the leap being built, on the days it happens.

    Ask your child

    Watch the crossing: card to apple, apple to card — how many trips today? Does the real apple’s smell or shine pull extra attention? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if you know the picture and the fruit are the same thing yet."

    What your child can say or do

    Gaze trips between card and fruit, a longer look at the real apple’s shine, an arm swing that grazes either one, or a calm study of both — every version is fine; the wiring does not need a visible reaction to grow.

    Out in the real world

    Apples ride through the week: in the fruit bowl, in your lunch, at the shop in a pyramid. Each sighting earns the word once. By the time your baby can grasp an apple, the word will already be an old friend.

    Try it together

    Fruit-bowl hello: once a day, lift the apple out of the bowl, say "apple" to your baby, and put it back. Thirty seconds, no card needed. The bowl becomes a daily page-turn of the world’s biggest picture book.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the real apple actually join the session, and did you resist the urge to add more fruit? One object, two forms, repeated — that is the whole method, and extra props only blur it.

    Parent tips

    If the real apple steals the show, let it — the card will be waiting tomorrow. Keep the fruit out of the session when it is bruised or cut; the card apple is always perfect, and the comparison works best when the real one looks its best.

    Staying safe

    Whole apples are far too hard for this age and stay in the fruit bowl, not the session. When solids begin months from now, apple arrives cooked or grated, never as a chunk — but that is another lesson; today is only about the name.

    This lesson pairs with the Apple flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & First Objects (Infant 1).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & FIRST OBJECTS · AGES 3–4 MONTHS

    Sun — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Babies meet the sun long before they meet its name: light through a window is one of the first moving things they ever watch. This lesson finally introduces the two.

    What is this?

    The sun is the bright thing in the sky that makes day, drawn here as a warm, smiling face. Your baby has been watching sunlight move across walls for months; the card gives that old friend a picture and a word.

    What does it mean?

    Sun is a vast abstraction made baby-sized: something too big to hold, met through a picture and a window. That is exactly what pictures are for — naming the ungrabbable. And the smiling version gives your baby a face in a place where the real one has none.

    What does the child need to know?

    The ritual is the lesson: on a bright day, carry the card to the window, glance at the light together and say "sun" once, softly. Never aim your baby’s eyes towards the sky itself — let the card carry the name while the window supplies gentle, indirect daylight.

    Why this matters

    Window-watching becomes conversation the moment it has words. "Sun" will be one of the first words your baby can connect to something far away — the first proof that words reach beyond arm’s length, into the sky itself.

    What it teaches

    Distant-object naming, light and shadow awareness, daily ritual building, and the emotional pairing of warm light with a warm word.

    Words to learn

    sunbrightskywarmlightday

    Say this to your child

    “"Sun! Here is the picture sun, smiling down. And look out the window — there is the real sun, way up high in the sky. It makes everything bright and warm. Hello, sun. Thank you for the daylight."”

    Step by step

    1. Pick a bright moment and show the card at close range first: "Sun. The bright, warm sun."
    2. Trace the smile and the rays with your finger while your baby studies the friendly face.
    3. Carry the card to the window where real light is coming in, and hold it beside the view — picture sun, window light.
    4. Say "sun" once, softly, looking out with your baby; then let the window hold the attention without more words.
    5. End by bringing the card back to your lap — the journey out and back is part of the ritual.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a warm, smiling sun with simple rays — say that much. The live noticing: on a bright day, does the window light collect a long look? Babies find moving light and shadows genuinely fascinating, and naming what they watch turns staring into conversation.

    Ask your child

    Watch the window: does your baby’s attention hold on the light outside, or return to the card’s friendly face? Does the same ritual spark faster each day? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if you know that bright thing is the same as this picture."

    What your child can say or do

    A long study of the window light, blinking happily at the brightness, a slow smile for the card’s sunny face, or drowsy eyelids — window light settles babies too, so keep the ritual short and bright, not long and glaring.

    Out in the real world

    The sun performs daily: morning light on the nursery wall, the bright patch on the kitchen floor, the view from the bus window. One word — "sun" — at any of these moments keeps the card echoing through every bright day.

    Try it together

    Light chase: when a sunbeam makes a bright patch on the floor, put your hand in it and say "sun", then lift your hand out and say "gone". Repeat. Your baby gets light, word and peek-a-boo logic in one tiny game.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the card actually visit the window today, and did you say the word just once or twice rather than on a loop? Sun is a once-a-day word; its power is in the pairing with real light, not the frequency.

    Parent tips

    Grey days are fine — the card still works, and the window ritual can be about the sky in general. Save the full sun pairing for the bright days; the contrast between the two makes the word itself feel like weather.

    Staying safe

    Real sun is for looking at indirectly, always — never position your baby so the sun shines into their eyes, and never use mirrors or phone screens to "show" it. The card names the sun; the window supplies safe, reflected light.

    This lesson pairs with the Sun flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & First Objects (Infant 1).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & FIRST OBJECTS · AGES 3–4 MONTHS

    Ball and cup — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Until now every card held one thing. Today it holds two — and this lesson turns that small change into a looking game your baby’s eyes have never played before.

    What is this?

    The ball and cup card shows two everyday objects sharing one page: the ball your baby has batted at, the cup they see at every feed. Both names are already known — the new part is the twoness.

    What does it mean?

    One-object cards ask the eyes to arrive and stay; two-object cards ask them to travel. The gaze must leave one thing to visit the other, and that leaving-and-arriving is the visual engine of scanning, comparing and, much later, reading across a line.

    What does the child need to know?

    The method is patient turns: name the ball, pause long enough for a real look, then name the cup, pause again. Two names, one card, and your baby’s eyes doing the walking between them. If the eyes only ever camp on one object, that is a fine day’s work too.

    Why this matters

    "More than one" is a quiet revolution in baby thinking — the moment a page, and by extension the world, stops being one thing at a time. Every later skill from counting to sharing a storybook runs on the ability to hold two things in view.

    What it teaches

    Multi-object scanning, gaze-shifting between targets, sequential naming with pauses, and consolidation of two already-learned words on a single card.

    Words to learn

    ballcuptwothisthatback and forth

    Say this to your child

    “"Look — two things on one card! Here is the ball... round and ready. And here is the cup... waiting for milk. Ball, cup. Back and forth, one and the other. Two friends sharing a page, just for you."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at close range and let your baby discover it is different today — two things! Name the card simply: "A ball and a cup."
    2. Name the ball first and point: "Ball." Then hold your finger still and give the gaze time to arrive.
    3. Shift to the cup: "Cup." Same patience — the pause is where the looking happens.
    4. Run the turns again, slower or faster on your baby’s mood, letting the eyes make their own trips between the two.
    5. End by naming both together — "ball and cup, two friends" — and bring the real cup or ball into view for a two-second cameo if attention allows.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork shows the two objects clearly separated on one page — say that much. The live noticing: how far do the eyes travel between the objects, and do the trips get longer through the session? Gaze-travel is the growth you can actually see.

    Ask your child

    Watch the journeys: does the gaze shuttle between ball and cup, or settle on a favourite? Does your pointing finger collect the eyes or do they roam alone? Wonder aloud: "I wonder which one is the home base today."

    What your child can say or do

    Shuttling looks between the two objects, a loyal stare on one with a glance for the other, excited arm movements when both real objects appear, or a fast loss of interest — two-object pages are bigger work, and shorter sessions are honest.

    Out in the real world

    Pairs fill the day: spoon and bowl, sock and foot, key and door. Naming real pairs — "spoon... bowl" — extends this card’s game to everything your baby already watches you handle.

    Try it together

    Two-object fetch: hold the real ball in one hand and the real cup in the other, bringing each into view as you name it, then both together. Card version, then live version — the same two objects wearing two costumes.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did you actually pause between the two names — a real pause, two or three seconds? The pause is the pedagogy; without it, two words blur into noise and the eyes lose their map.

    Parent tips

    If your baby always looks at the same object first, say that one second — follow their order rather than imposing yours. The card teaches turn-taking, but your baby gets to call the coin toss.

    Staying safe

    Two real props means twice the grab-management: hands stay behind both objects, and neither rests within reach on the mat. If both objects end up fought over, the game worked — retire it for today rather than refereeing.

    This lesson pairs with the Ball and cup flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & First Objects (Infant 1).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & FIRST OBJECTS · AGES 3–4 MONTHS

    Teddy bear — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Most sets have one card that makes a baby’s whole face change, and this is usually it: the card that looks like someone they know. This lesson makes the introduction formal.

    What is this?

    A teddy bear is a soft toy friend, and for many babies this card names an actual resident of the cot corner or the shelf. The picture is not a stranger — it is a portrait session for someone already loved.

    What does it mean?

    Comfort objects carry enormous emotional weight, and words attached to them get processed with the volume turned up. Naming the teddy fuses language with security — some of the strongest glue a first vocabulary can have.

    What does the child need to know?

    The procedure is a proper hello: show the card, then fetch the real bear for a side-by-side meeting — the picture bear, the fur bear, and your delighted voice joining the two. If teddy starts attending every card session from now on, that is not a distraction; it is a ritual being born.

    Why this matters

    Routines with a comfort object teach more than the word: they teach that looking-time is safe time. A baby who does card time with teddy beside them gets the word, the picture and the calm — and calm babies look longer.

    What it teaches

    Emotional security during learning, word-object mapping for a beloved object, soft-touch sensory experience, and routine-building — the same faces and words in the same warm order.

    Words to learn

    teddybearsoftcuddlyhellohug

    Say this to your child

    “"Teddy bear! Look, here is teddy on the card... and here is YOUR teddy, come to say hello. Soft teddy, cuddly teddy. Shall we let teddy watch card time with us? Hello, teddy. Welcome to the class."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at close range with a warm voice: "Teddy bear! You know this friend."
    2. Let your baby study the picture, then reach for the real teddy and bring it into view beside the card.
    3. Introduce them properly: "Card teddy, meet real teddy" — and let the real bear nod and wave with your hand doing the honours.
    4. Bring the real teddy close for a touch against your baby’s hands or cheek — soft is the whole point of teddy.
    5. Seat the real teddy where it can "watch" the rest of the session, and let that be its job from now on.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a soft, friendly teddy bear — say that much. The live noticing is the meeting: does your baby’s gaze travel between the picture bear and the real one? And does the touch of soft fur change their body language? Comfort shows on babies as loosening.

    Ask your child

    Watch the recognition: does your baby look from card to bear with fresh interest, or treat them as two unrelated things? Wonder aloud: "I wonder when you will start smiling at teddy’s name alone."

    What your child can say or do

    Bright-eyed looks that swing between card and bear, fingers curling into the fur, a whole-body snuggle when teddy arrives, or a gummy smile aimed at your teddy-voice — any of these means the friendship is doing its work.

    Out in the real world

    Teddy lives everywhere your baby goes: the cot, the car seat, grandma’s spare that lives at grandma’s house. Each sighting is a replay — "teddy" — and this card may end up the most-repeated word in the whole set.

    Try it together

    Teddy says hello: let the bear greet your baby by name each session — "hello, little one" — in your teddy-voice, then touch paws gently to their hands. Two greetings, two voices, one friend. It never gets old at this age.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the real teddy actually attend the session, and did the meeting get words — an introduction, not just proximity? The naming is what turns a prop into a character.

    Parent tips

    If your family has no teddy, the closest soft thing works — a comfort cloth, a plush anything. The lesson is about naming a loved object, not this exact bear. Keep the teddy-voice consistent; babies recognise voices before faces.

    Staying safe

    Choose the session teddy with baby-safety eyes: no glued-on buttons or bead eyes, no loose ribbon neckwear, nothing that sheds fibres. Soft toys that live in the cot stay out of card time if they are sleep-only friends — card time can borrow a different bear.

    This lesson pairs with the Teddy bear flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & First Objects (Infant 1).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & FIRST OBJECTS · AGES 3–4 MONTHS

    Simple face — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The set ends where babies’ interest never ends: a face. This lesson uses the last card to look at the picture, then look at each other — and to begin the whole set again tomorrow.

    What is this?

    A simple face is a clear, friendly human face, drawn boldly — the kind of image babies never stop finding interesting. After circles, objects and a bear, the set closes on the thing your baby has loved longest: faces, especially yours.

    What does it mean?

    Faces outlast every other visual interest in infancy because they carry everything social — attention, emotion, conversation. Ending the set here is a quiet statement: all the colour and object words in the world lead back to people.

    What does the child need to know?

    The finish is a hand-off: study the picture, then offer your own face at the same distance, holding a warm expression. Your baby looks from card to you and back — the comparison is theirs to make, and it ends the set with a person, not a page.

    Why this matters

    This card completes a loop that started in the very first face cards weeks ago: your baby has met faces, patterns, colours, objects and friends, and now meets a face again — but a slightly different baby is doing the looking. Progress in infancy looks like the same lesson, seen by new eyes.

    What it teaches

    Face preference (the strongest visual interest babies have), card-to-person transfer, social attention, and consolidation of the whole set into one warm final session.

    Words to learn

    facehelloeyessmileall doneagain

    Say this to your child

    “"A face! One friendly face on the very last card. Look at the eyes... the smile... And now look here — MY face, just like the picture, smiling at you. We did all our cards, little one. Tomorrow we begin again."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at close range with a settled voice: "A face. The last card of our set."
    2. Tour it simply — the eyes, the mouth, the friendly whole — with one touch each and no hurry.
    3. Then the hand-off: bring your own face to the same distance, smiling warmly, and let your baby look between card and parent.
    4. Answer any smile, coo or stare with your own quiet delight — this is a conversation, and you are the other half.
    5. Close the set out loud: "We finished our cards! We will start them again tomorrow." Then put them away, visibly, together.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a clear, friendly face in bold simple features — say that much. The live noticing is the hand-off: when your face replaces the card, does the attention follow? Faces usually win that contest, and watching it happen is the set’s final experiment.

    Ask your child

    Watch the transfer: does the gaze move from card to your face, or does one hold it completely? Does the closing line — the same words each time — start to mean "finished"? Wonder aloud: "I wonder how much your looking has changed since the first card."

    What your child can say or do

    Long mutual gazing once your face takes over, a full social smile, cooing that turns into a duet, or a tired but content blink — the last card of a set often gets the best conversation, because everything today is already familiar.

    Out in the real world

    Faces run the whole world your baby lives in: yours at every feed, siblings at play, strangers at the shop leaning in. The card’s word — "face" — is one your baby will hear attached to real examples a hundred times this month.

    Try it together

    Card-and-me: hold the card beside your own face at equal distance and let your baby’s eyes choose; then swap sides, then hide the card entirely. The game ends when the card is gone and only your face remains — which was always the ending it deserved.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the set actually get its closing ceremony — the last card, the hand-off, the words? Endings honour beginnings, and tomorrow’s restart will be easier because today finished properly.

    Parent tips

    Restarting the set is not repeating it — at 4 months your baby will meet these same twelve cards with new abilities: stronger gaze, real reaches, maybe laughs. Keep the restart date and treat it as a graduation, not a loop.

    Staying safe

    Close-quarters face time is safest with a settled, supported baby — no leaning over a crying baby to force the moment. Cards go away with you as always; the set that lives in its box is the set that survives to be restarted.

    This lesson pairs with the Simple face flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & First Objects (Infant 1).
